```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7)
library(BlackThriveSS)
# Data frames returned by a chunk render as tables in the vignette and on the website.
library(knitr)
registerS3method("knit_print", "data.frame", function(x, ...) {
  asis_output(paste(c("", kable(x, row.names = FALSE), ""), collapse = "\n"))
})
```

This vignette is for people who need to say something accurate about stop
and search in one place: a police force area or a council. It needs no
statistics beyond reading the statements the package writes, and nothing
here requires a network connection.

## One call for the evidence

```{r profile}
p <- btg_profile(force = "metropolitan", draws = 500)
p
```

Each statement carries its own qualification: the interval, the rank and
how far sampling alone could move it, how far the stops with no recorded
ethnicity could move the ratio, whether both years of a change were covered
in full. The tables behind the statements are in the object:

```{r tables}
p$comparisons[c("group", "ratio", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "rank", "n_eligible", "rank_lower", "rank_upper", "parity_direction")]
p$change[c("group", "ratio_from", "ratio_to", "change", "change_direction", "comparable_coverage")]
p$coverage[c("status", "months_supplied", "months_missing")]
```

A council profile works the same way, without ranks or coverage, because
council counts depend on published stop coordinates:

```{r council}
btg_profile(council = "E09000022", draws = 500)$statements[1:3]
```

## The charts a briefing needs

The ranking chart with the area highlighted, as on the dashboard:

```{r ranking, fig.alt = "Black to White stop-rate ratios for the ten highest forces in 2025 with the Metropolitan Police highlighted."}
year <- btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", years = 2025)
btg_plot_disparity(year, highlight = "metropolitan")
```

The same comparisons with their uncertainty shown honestly:

```{r robust, fig.alt = "Recorded ratios with sampling intervals and bounds under unknown ethnicity, Metropolitan Police highlighted."}
btg_plot_sensitivity(year, highlight = "metropolitan")
```

How the area's ratios have moved, with incomplete periods marked:

```{r trend, fig.alt = "Metropolitan Police stop-rate ratios by group and year."}
met <- btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", force = "metropolitan")
btg_plot_trend(met)
```

Rates per 1,000 residents with one group emphasised and the rest as context:

```{r rates, fig.alt = "Recorded stops per 1,000 residents by group for the Metropolitan Police, Black emphasised."}
btg_plot_trend(met, measure = "rate", highlight = "Black")
```

National context: the share of recorded stops by group, month by month, and
the outcome-linked search rate by group.

```{r national, fig.alt = "Share of recorded stops by ethnic group across England and Wales by month."}
btg_plot_trend(btg_get_data("national_month_ethnicity"), measure = "share")
btg_plot_trend(btg_get_data("hit_rate_ethnicity_year"))
```

## A complete briefing in one file

`btg_report()` renders a self-contained HTML briefing from the package's
installed R Markdown template: the statements, the charts above, the tables
behind them, monthly coverage, the methods and their limits, and the code
and citations that reproduce every figure. It needs the rmarkdown package
and Pandoc, which RStudio and Positron include.

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
btg_report(force = "metropolitan", file = "metropolitan-2025.html")
btg_report(council = "E09000022", year = 2024, file = "lambeth-2024.docx")
btg_report(force = "kent", year = 2024, file = "kent-2024.pdf")
```

A `.docx` file name, or `format = "docx"`, gives the same briefing as a
Word document for people who need to edit it or paste from it, styled by a
reference document installed with the template; `.pdf` gives a PDF where a
LaTeX installation such as TinyTeX is available. The briefing opens with an
at-a-glance panel and the findings grouped by topic, and numbers its tables
and figures. `btg_table()` sets any data frame in the same style inside your
own R Markdown document, whichever of the three formats you knit to:

```{r table}
btg_table(head(btg_get_data("national_year")$data[c("year", "stops", "arrest_rate", "hit_rate")]),
          caption = "National totals by year")
```

The template is also listed in those editors under *New R Markdown, From
Template* as "BlackThriveSS briefing", for anyone who wants to add their own
sections.

## Taking numbers out of R

`btg_export()` writes a dataset to CSV with a JSON sidecar that records the
release, checksums, selection, citation and limitations:

```{r export}
csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
files <- btg_export(btg_get_data(force = "metropolitan"), csv)
basename(files)
unlink(files)
```

And every term the package uses has one definition:

```{r glossary}
g <- btg_glossary()
g[g$term %in% c("ratio", "allocation range", "coverage"), ]
```

## Saying it right

A few rules that the statements follow and that are worth keeping in any
briefing built on them:

* Say *recorded stops per 1,000 residents*, not the chance of being stopped.
  Residents stand in for the people present in an area.
* Give the interval and the allocation range with the ratio, and the
  coverage with any change.
* Ranks move a long way under sampling alone; quote the rank interval.
* A ratio describes recorded stops relative to population. It does not,
  by itself, show discrimination, and it does not separate recording
  practice, who is present and policing decisions.
